j2ywddv A camera with film
7yd180f Look at the camera. It used real film, developed on board.
ds1r1cr In 1966, Lunar Orbiter 1 photographed areas of the Moon where the Apollo missions might land. Its camera used film, which the spacecraft developed and sent to Earth by radio. With those photos, the teams looked for smooth, safe ground before the astronauts arrived.
qkrz5w4 Earth on the horizon
7peaebh Open the restored photo. This is how Earth looked from the Moon in 1966.
czl5cm0 The camera also captured Earth above the lunar horizon. After finishing its work, the spacecraft was steered toward the surface and crashed on October 29, 1966. Decades later, a team recovered the image from the original recordings and removed most of the lines seen in the first version.
d0qh1am Earth above the lunar horizon, in the version restored in 2008.

ymdw1kl Safe places to land
oz233fn It photographed the nine sites planned for the Apollo landings and 11 more places on the far side. Together with the other Lunar Orbiters, it helped choose where the Apollo missions would land.
fi72idt Earth seen from the Moon
p5fafex On August 23, 1966, it took the first photo of Earth from near the Moon. It wasn't in the main plan. The engineers turned the spacecraft to take it.
xsy0642 Photos recovered decades later
mqp6r0n It exposed 205 frames covering about 5 million km². In 2008, a project recovered the original tapes and restored the photos in much higher quality.
7cb38ro The probe the astronauts came back to visit
7tikst9 A scoop to test the ground
lag6ynn Look at the scoop. It dug trenches and pressed on the soil.
crb4kgf In 1969, two Apollo 12 astronauts walked over to Surveyor 3, which had been sitting in a lunar crater for more than two years. Its scoop had dug trenches and pressed on the ground to measure how firm it was. That told the engineers whether the ground could hold the weight of a spacecraft.
b4q797e Parts that came back to Earth
dv9mpmi Find the camera on the model. The astronauts took it apart and brought it home.
dq2q650 The astronauts removed the camera and the scoop and brought them to Earth. Researchers could study how the equipment had changed during its stay on the Moon. The rest of the probe stayed in the crater.

2mzixy2 An Apollo 12 astronaut next to Surveyor 3. Their lunar module is in the background.
k4usbi7 Most of the probe, in its crater in Oceanus Procellarum.

fizl702 Its television images and the studies of the recovered parts.
dkc0zlj Photo and recovered parts · NASA
lu3p8vq Soil tests · NASA
oxznyqd Thousands of images of the terrain
db1nwn8 It sent 6,326 television images of the lunar surface, which helped the Apollo engineers get to know the terrain. It even photographed an eclipse, with Earth blocking the Sun.
okvv5tr Ground as firm as wet sand
jg75a20 Its scoop dug four trenches and showed that lunar soil behaved like wet sand. That confirmed a crewed spacecraft could land without sinking.
okrf8em Parts that came home
kvyccm4 In 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts recovered its camera and scoop to study how being on the Moon had affected them. Some thought bacteria from Earth had survived in the camera. Today it's believed it got contaminated on the way back.
p44eflh The part of Eagle that stayed on the Moon
9ydpstt The descent engine
h7mw7nz Look at the gold part at the bottom. Its engine slowed the descent.
ya6kz31 On July 20, 1969, the engine between Eagle's four legs slowed the descent of Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin toward the Sea of Tranquility. That part of the module later served as a launch pad and stayed on the surface.
8guflhu The complete Eagle lunar module on the ground of the Sea of Tranquility
c1b4lw9 The complete Eagle on the Moon, before liftoff. Afterwards, only the descent stage stayed at the site.
b87tctj This cabin lifted off with its own engine. Tap «Surface equipment» to see what stayed behind.
mhavbkx Ascent cabin
cvusnnl Surface equipment
l9hh7zz The upper cabin lifted off with its own engine and docked in lunar orbit with Columbia, where Michael Collins was waiting. The three astronauts returned to Earth aboard Columbia with the lunar samples. At the landing site they left a reflector used to measure the distance between Earth and the Moon.
5ly3bcl The descent stage and the surface equipment, including the laser reflector. Eagle's cabin was released in lunar orbit and this archive does not confirm its final fate.
o3ezos5 The samples, which are still being studied, and the mission's photos and films.
5yw9doy Mission report · NASA
bs64kuq Lunar reflectors · NASA
d9pj0ca Samples for the lab
2eto591 They brought about 22 kg of lunar rock and dust back to Earth. The samples were shared among scientists from many countries and are still being studied.
d9w9wjv The age of the Moon
yur7q33 The samples helped show that the Moon is about 4.5 billion years old and chemically similar to Earth. That similarity supports the idea that it formed after a giant collision with the young Earth.
gn1zwxe A reflector that still works
s0w9hjy From Earth, a laser is fired at the reflector they left, and scientists measure how long the light takes to come back. Thanks to it we know the Moon drifts away about 3.8 cm per year.
uwbge5a The first car ride on the Moon
5y6y0q0 Mesh wheels
ch63uv8 Look at the mesh wheels. They didn't need air and couldn't get a flat.
tb8kojr In 1971, David Scott and James Irwin unfolded the first vehicle astronauts ever drove on the Moon. Its mesh wheels and electric motors let them cross the terrain at Hadley, get farther from the lunar module and carry tools to collect samples in several places.
17icx1h The Genesis Rock
akl7k8t Look at the back. That's where the tools and sample bags rode.
vlrxyuj At one stop they found the Genesis Rock, a light-colored piece of the ancient lunar crust that gave clues about the Moon's earliest days. The rock traveled to Earth to be studied in the lab. The rover stayed at Hadley.
o2309x9 The samples, including the Genesis Rock.
6oy3u96 The mission's photos, films and sample catalog.
pzxo9mp Genesis Rock and route · NASA
fqj1tcj The first car on the Moon
0ponx5y It was the first vehicle astronauts drove on the Moon. They covered 27.8 km, visited more places than they could on foot and brought back about 77 kg of samples.
iklupet A piece of the first crust
b1kgtw2 They found the Genesis Rock, a piece of anorthosite more than 4 billion years old. It supported the idea that the young Moon was covered by an ocean of molten rock.
0qs1hpy What appeared when the dust settled
br5dp8g Mars under the dust
xe7vu5l Look at the camera platform. With it they saw Olympus Mons poke through.
fqro9nx When Mariner 9 reached Mars in 1971, a dust storm covered almost the whole surface. While it waited, its cameras photographed the moons Phobos and Deimos. Only a few peaks poked out of the dust, like the top of the volcano Olympus Mons.
x7vvhdo Mariner 9 on Earth, before a thermal vacuum test. This is not a photo of Mars.
6cr025k Volcanoes, canyons and channels
y9frp1g Spin the model until you see the cameras from below. Its photos guided the Vikings.
xux4htc Photos of Mars taken by Mariner 9 · NASA
m20ndqt When the dust settled, the photos showed huge volcanoes, canyons and channels suggesting that water once flowed there. Mariner 9 mapped about 85% of the surface and helped choose where the Vikings would land. It stopped operating in 1972 and its final fate in orbit is still open.
hxij1ka The spacecraft stayed in orbit around Mars. Predictions about when it leaves orbit keep its final fate open.
tpf6qk1 No parts. Its images came by radio.
246heqx The photos it used to map about 85% of the surface.
99rczl7 History and photographs · NASA
wkt312n Expected fate · JPL
loyybrf The first map of Mars
77pj1g6 It took 7,329 photos and covered about 85% of the surface. It was the first global map of Mars and helped choose where the Vikings would land.
o9oxlah A canyon the size of a continent
0dskzh8 It discovered a huge canyon system that was named Valles Marineris in its honor. It is more than 4,000 km long.
m1o13e8 Volcanoes above the storm
0mb1wjh During the dust storm only four dark spots could be seen. They were giant volcanoes, and Olympus Mons is the largest known in the solar system.
fsa1kco Moons up close and dry riverbeds

vphs853 It photographed the moons Phobos and Deimos up close. It also saw channels suggesting that water once flowed, so Mars wasn't always a dry desert.
7imu8bb The rocks of Descartes changed the explanation
0x8ydda Heading for the highlands
yhrefai Look at the wheels. They took the crew to very different spots around Descartes.
41mnvr4 Before Apollo 16, images of the Descartes highlands made people think volcanoes had shaped part of the landscape. In 1972, John Young and Charles Duke used their rover to cross the area and collect samples at different points.
ga9vx4v The LRV-2 at Descartes, next to the lunar module Orion.
8jwozfm Rocks made by impacts
ryi3k0g Spin the model while you read. The rocks this rover brought back changed the explanation.
7m9m2w9 Apollo 16 sample catalog · NASA
9oeuawc Many of the rocks they found were made of pieces of other rocks that stuck together after big impacts. The samples made it possible to rethink what had been read from the photos. The vehicle stayed at Descartes and the samples reached Earth so other teams could study that ground.
ejwishx The mission's photos and sample catalog.
wyy6g19 Sample catalog · NASA
glyhhtk More places in less time
4qu4kwe With the rover, the astronauts traveled 26.7 km across the highlands. They visited craters like North Ray and the slopes of Stone Mountain, and brought back rocks from very different areas.
j47bqwf Impacts, not volcanoes
h25lhj5 From far away, the highlands looked like they were made by volcanoes. Almost everything turned out to be rock broken and stuck together by impacts. It was a lesson not to trust only what you see from a distance.
ftotpeb A fender made of maps
qt0c0n6 Maps as a fender
698b5ha Look at the right rear wheel. The maps rode on top of it.
z83eayp See the LRV-3 demonstrations
79ofr0w During Apollo 17, the rover lost part of its right rear fender and the wheel threw dust over the equipment. The astronauts clamped several maps over the wheel. Those maps worked as a fender for the rest of the drive.
tpc6cel The LRV-3 in the Taurus–Littrow valley.
8fsk6f2 Orange glass at Shorty
zrwai63 Spin the rover. It took them all the way to Shorty crater.
cwgs1i9 Fender repair · Apollo 17 report
mzu5gga Orange soil sample · NASA
tma7i65 With the rover, the crew visited interesting spots in the Taurus–Littrow valley. Near Shorty crater they collected orange grains that turned out to be glass from ancient lunar eruptions. When the work was done, the vehicle stayed parked in the valley.
ofb47lm The rover, parked in the Taurus–Littrow valley.
0qdlxzk The mission report, photos, films and the sample catalog.
d1scb6e Repair and image · Apollo 17 report
hzpguxb Orange sample · NASA
ft5gzbs The longest Apollo drive
f3v12ml Thanks to the rover, the astronauts traveled 35.9 km in three outings and got as far as 7.6 km from the lunar module. It was the longest distance covered in the Apollo missions.
istejmt Orange glass next to Shorty crater
x3mpnwi Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, noticed the orange color of the soil next to Shorty crater. They were tiny drops of glass from ancient lava fountains, more than 3.5 billion years old. They showed that the Moon once had explosive eruptions.
8m0pf8j A leg on Mars and a question about life
9ea31fl A leg in the photo
aws92zn Look at the cylindrical cameras. One of them photographed the leg.
u01g04o The first photograph from Mars · NASA
by42dej Shortly after reaching Chryse Planitia in 1976, Viking 1 took a photograph showing one of its own legs. Scientists could see the stones, the dust and the ground around the station. Over the following years, the lander sent images and weather measurements.
nuprmrv Viking 1 hardware during integration on Earth, before launch. This is not a photo of Mars.
6q8gbox The arm brought soil to this lab. Tap «Sampling arm» to see it.
edzl8wm Biology lab
85gvhmk Biology results · NASA
w0w3tt6 Its arm scooped up soil and carried it to instruments looking for signs of biological activity. The results were read in different ways and life was never confirmed. The surface module stayed at Chryse Planitia and its images and measurements were kept on Earth.
29gmkua The surface module, at Chryse Planitia.
989e9db Its images and its measurements of the weather and the soil.
ly12v8z First photograph and context · NASA
pi4rhcz The first color photos from the ground
hv2lgcf It sent the first color photo of the surface of Mars. It showed a reddish landscape full of rocks and a sky tinted ochre by dust.
o08euv3 An unconfirmed answer
sz5rlxj One experiment gave the soil nutrients with labeled carbon to see if anything ate them. There was a positive signal, but another instrument found no organic molecules and life was never confirmed. Later studies suggest the soil may have held organic matter that wasn't detected.
b06tgok Six years instead of three months
danjt5c Its nuclear generators gave it power day and night. It worked until November 1982, more than six years, and its surface record lasted until 2010.
smw7u6o Frost among the rocks of Utopia Planitia
6xvso13 Frost among the rocks
j5m347b Look at the surface module. Its cameras photographed the frost.
gnz1av7 Viking 2 landed farther north than Viking 1 to compare the soil and weather of two regions of Mars. In winter, its camera showed patches of frost among the rocks of Utopia Planitia. The photos and temperatures helped explain how the frost formed.
l97qxmr White frost among the rocks at the Viking 2 site in Utopia Planitia
5lmutf5 Frost at the Viking 2 site, photographed by the surface module.
lyfnxux Two vehicles, one team
hw9g15l This is the orbiter. Tap «Surface module» to go back to the one that took the photos.
0rc9lnf Surface module
t7ld9wb The mission had two vehicles. The surface module photographed the frost and studied the soil, while the orbiter watched Mars from above and relayed data. The module stayed at Utopia Planitia when its operations ended.
7d0fp93 The surface module, at Utopia Planitia. This archive does not include the orbiter's current position.
58u22r4 Frost photo · JPL
fqjw4qx Viking Project · NASA
jx1mt70 Frost at Utopia Planitia
0l7yg9i In winter, the camera photographed a very thin layer of frost on the ground. Measuring the weather in two places so far apart helped explain the climate of the whole planet.
nhhbdur Soil that puzzled the experiments
hoq9h2n The biology experiments looked for microbes that would eat nutrients or give off gases. The confusing results showed that Martian soil is chemically very reactive, and life was never confirmed.
vwot7d6 Power for years
fzrt71g Its nuclear generators didn't depend on sunlight. Thanks to them, the module worked for about three and a half years instead of three months.
fvdqhpc From the rock Yogi to Earth
xnspfwc A rover at Ares Vallis
n8l729e Spin Sojourner. It arrived folded up inside the Pathfinder module.
jjmhtg2 In 1997, the Pathfinder module carried a small six-wheeled robot called Sojourner to Mars. Once at Ares Vallis, the module opened its petals and the rover rolled down a ramp. That way it could show that a vehicle sent from Earth could move around Mars and study its ground.
a6ylpvi The rock Yogi
01tmhb4 Look at the back. That's where the APXS it placed on Yogi rides.
xt5o4mi Sojourner carried an instrument called the APXS on its back and placed it on the rock Yogi to find out what it was made of. The first measurements showed that Yogi looked like certain volcanic rocks on Earth. The Pathfinder module photographed the rover and acted as a bridge to send its data to Earth.
shid11e Sojourner, with its six wheels, next to the rock Yogi at Ares Vallis
dfwbcdr Sojourner with the APXS resting on Yogi, photographed by the Pathfinder module between sols 8 and 10.
avt9him NASA/JPL · «Sojourner & Yogi», PIA00766
amz0tlu Last contact and official end
orshwg2 Data went out to the module through this antenna. From there it traveled to Earth.
r3sdbkr Send your own commands to Mars
b6bk1qq APXS data in NASA's archive (PDS)
zdu6h9l Pathfinder sent its last data transmission in September 1997 and the mission was declared over in March 1998. The module and the rover stayed at Ares Vallis. Their data is kept in NASA's archive.
wpnjlyx The Pathfinder module and Sojourner, at Ares Vallis.
oux1q5w No parts. The data came by radio through the module.
byyjxo0 The images and the APXS measurements, in NASA's planetary archive (PDS).

gahavn7 The signal that never came
n8o5f0q The viewer shows a 3D reconstruction. Nobody saw the probes after their planned arrival.

q0zsxlk Probes to look below the ground
tprxm29 Look at the penetrator. It was meant to drive into the Martian ground.
ugr1a73 Cable
z95ojuf Scott and Amundsen were two small probes designed to reach a place a surface camera can't see. They were meant to drive into the ground near the south pole of Mars and look for water in the buried material. After impact, a cable would have connected the buried piece to the part above ground that carried the battery and the antenna.
7az3mdk The signal was supposed to come from this part. It never arrived.
7v2fora The two probes traveled with Mars Polar Lander, but when it was time to receive their signal, nothing came. Without data, nobody could confirm whether the design worked on Mars. Their exact location and the cause of the loss are still unconfirmed.
mpkjcdx The two probes, somewhere near the south pole of Mars. Their exact location is unknown.
ixtialo No parts and no data from Mars.
5f1dkbk The design documents, the photos of the flight hardware and the report on the loss.
as4ejdr Deep Space 2 and loss report · NASA
1phpkau After the planned arrival on December 3, 1999, no signal was received from Scott or Amundsen. The probes could only transmit after driving into the ground, so there was no data from the fall. That's why missions today try to send information during the descent.
825u75l A loss with no witnesses
a90sy04 Nobody saw them fall and there were no cameras in the area. The cause of the loss and the exact place where they landed are still unknown.
t98wq76 Technology for the future
dcip289 They were part of the New Millennium program, which tested new technologies, like small probes that drive into the ground to look for water. The ideas of shrinking instruments and surviving hard impacts kept being used in other projects.
zvqach3 The wheel that uncovered a clue about water
ed476vh A wheel that stopped turning
rslmahg Look at the front right wheel. As it dragged, it dug a trench.
a77xvn0 Spirit's wheel track, PIA11758 · NASA
nlydvt3 One of Spirit's front wheels stopped turning and, as it dragged, it dug a small trench. The track uncovered bright soil very rich in silica. The rover studied that material and photographed the mark left by its wheel.
r53f7vt Clues about water
h2m40bb It studied the bright soil with the instruments on this arm.
uobr8zu The silica may have built up in hot springs or with volcanic steam, and both point to there having been water in that part of Mars. Years later, Spirit got stuck in soft ground. The rover is still there and its measurements are kept on Earth.
vu1ipml The rover, stuck in soft ground in Gusev crater.
vb2sv9m Its photos and measurements, including those of the silica-rich soil.
7vkmp4c Spirit's wheel track · NASA
5izcefr The track of a stuck wheel
zcfvmck Look at the front right wheel. It's the one that dug the trench.
7b67dpn A front wheel jammed and, as it was dragged, it churned up the soil. Underneath was a bright material made almost entirely of silica, which on Earth forms in hot springs or with volcanic steam.
0g18av5 Rocks with carbonate
evdrie0 In the rocks called Comanche it found lots of carbonate. That shows the water of ancient Mars wasn't always acidic.
tfy0ys9 Places with warm water
yuzalnq Putting the silica and the carbonates together, scientists pictured places with warm water in Mars's past. On Earth, environments like those are home to microbes. That doesn't prove there was life on Mars.
yt5r9bh Much farther than planned
6cbkjho The plan was to drive about 600 meters in 90 sols, and it drove 7.73 km. In 2009 it got stuck in soft sand and kept working as a stationary station until 2010.
v4wqx0h The storm that cut the journey short
3j23yyg Layers and hematite spheres
zcfqsin Look at the arm. It studied rocks up close with its instruments.
zc8szbd Arm
ma21ye6 Opportunity landed at Meridiani Planum to study minerals linked to water. In the rocks it found layers and tiny spheres rich in hematite. Together with other minerals the rover measured, those observations helped rebuild a time when liquid water flowed over that ground.
pu7i4t6 The storm
hlxo31i Look at the panels. The storm took away their light.
a7hmyki Opportunity's last image, incomplete · NASA
8kmm0jj It traveled more than 45 km and worked for more than 14 years. In June 2018, a storm darkened the sky, its panels got very little light and one of its last images arrived incomplete. Opportunity stayed in Perseverance Valley and NASA closed the mission in 2019, after trying to restore contact.
1n37uqa Hematite spheres
9cmkny1 At its landing site it found tiny hematite spheres, nicknamed «blueberries». That mineral usually forms with water, which is why the rover landed right there.
or4pfja Layers that were once soaked
masp9nz The rocks in Eagle crater had thin layers and jarosite, a mineral that forms in water. In 2004, NASA announced that the place had been soaked long ago.
5ee0pwv A distance record
0g0sigm It traveled more than 45 km to reach older rocks, like those on the rim of Endeavour crater. In 2014 it passed Lunokhod 2 and became the vehicle that had traveled farthest off Earth.
gz95lzz Panels cleaned by the wind
unnlzfi Dust was expected to cover its panels within a few months, but the wind cleaned them from time to time. Designed for 90 Martian days, it worked for more than 14 years.
e4aan91 The ice Phoenix found under the dust
46hzbhb A trench in the north of Mars
gpb6ey5 Look at the arm. It dug the trench where the bright bits appeared.
q0pjqum The trench before and after, PIA10911 · JPL
uiau6i0 From orbit, Mars Odyssey had seen signs of ice in the north of Mars, and Phoenix landed there in 2008 to check. Its arm dug a trench and uncovered some bright bits. Four days later, the camera looked again and the bits were gone.
lbn0a9q The scoop on Phoenix's arm, upside down, photographed on Mars
8tuu938 The scoop on Phoenix's arm, seen on Mars. It used it to dig the trenches.
e2o07c7 The ice sublimated
fyg7l9g Here, in TEGA's ovens, they heated the soil.
zrxtr68 The ice had gone straight from solid to vapor. Phoenix also heated a soil sample in one of its small ovens and detected water vapor. That way, the mission confirmed from the surface a clue that had been spotted from orbit.
cc3k4tg Winter
fef3cxl Look at the panels. In winter they got very little light.
henceit As the Martian winter approached, the panels got less light and Phoenix stopped transmitting. The module stayed in the north of Mars. The photographs let us compare what its camera saw before and after the ice disappeared.
u1wvtlk The landing module, on the northern plains of Mars.
67545s3 The before-and-after photos of the trench, and the data from its ovens and its lab.
pedeu03 Trench comparison · JPL
yp8fgc7 Mission and results · NASA
rrcj248 Ice that vanished from the trench
neat9qe Some bright chunks the arm uncovered in a trench disappeared within a few days. The ice had sublimated, which means it went from solid to vapor. Then the TEGA oven detected water vapor and confirmed the clue Mars Odyssey had seen from orbit.
5i3y9rg An unexpected salt
gtjrk98 The MECA lab mixed soil with water and found perchlorate, a chemical compound that was the mission's big surprise. Its presence changed how the Viking results were interpreted.
cayu1rr Soil that may have gotten wet
sfrtqsy Heating the soil in the oven revealed calcium carbonate. On Earth it forms with liquid water, so Martian soil may have gotten damp from time to time.
moqxd6j Snow from the clouds
qy7seyu The LIDAR, a laser pointed at the sky, detected snow falling from Martian clouds. It evaporated before reaching the ground.
0eeuf8k An instrument to listen to the inside of Mars
1r1viog A seismometer on the ground
an8sfx6 Look at the SEIS dome. Tap «Arm» to see how they placed it.
c0przkw SEIS
vbb7785 InSight's arm placed a seismometer on the ground of Mars. The instrument, called SEIS, recorded vibrations caused by quakes and impacts. By studying how the waves changed as they crossed the planet, scientists could estimate what its inner layers were like.
fyp9m9k Look at the round panels. Dust slowly covered them.
tjge6xf Dust piled up on the solar panels and the available power dropped. InSight sent its last communication in December 2022 and stayed at Elysium Planitia. The SEIS records were made available so other teams could keep studying the Martian interior.
53nn7vs The landing module and its SEIS seismometer, at Elysium Planitia.
3s2yghb End of mission and results of InSight · JPL
jgy82a2 Revision of the interior model · Nature
n9azk03 Mars still shakes
rm5wbuf SEIS recorded 1,319 marsquakes, including some caused by meteoroid strikes. The largest, in May 2022, had a magnitude of 4.7. That proved Mars is still active inside.
wths33r An X-ray of the interior
8rxfyfz Quake waves change depending on the material they pass through, and with them scientists estimated what the crust, mantle and core of Mars are like. An initial estimate gave the core a radius of about 1,830 km. That size depends on the model used and later studies revised it.
1wltva2 Impacts that revealed ice
a25iba3 SEIS also recorded meteoroid impacts, and counting new craters helps work out the age of the surface. One of the biggest, in 2021, uncovered blocks of ice closer to the equator than had been seen before.
